messages.content: What is the freezing point point of water at a pressure of 10 kPa?

message.content:
**Answer**

At a pressure of **10 kPa**, the freezing (melting) point of pure water is practically the same as under normal‑atmospheric conditions:

| Pressure | Freezing Point |
|----------|----------------|
| 10 kPa   | –0.02 °C (≈ 0 °C) |

---

### Why the freezing point hardly moves

Water’s triple point—the unique combination of temperature and pressure at which ice, liquid water, and vapor all coexist—is located at  

\[
p_{\text{triple}} \;\approx\; 611.66\ \text{Pa}\;(0.006\,\text{atm}), \qquad 
T_{\text{triple}}\;\approx\;-0.01^\circ\text{C}.
\]

Below \(p_{\text{triple}}\) ice cannot exist in equilibrium with liquid water; instead it sublimes directly into vapor.  
Above \(p_{\text{triple}}\) an equilibrium exists between ice and liquid, and the melting/freeze line runs almost horizontally across the pressure axis—only a tiny fraction of a degree per kilobar.

A quick calculation based on the Clausius–Clapeyron relation gives

\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}P}
\simeq \frac{L_\text{fus}}{T\,\Delta v},
\]
where \(L_\text{fus}=333.55\ \text{kJ·kg}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta v\approx -9\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}^3\!\cdot\! \text{kg}^{-1}\).
This yields a slope of roughly \(+0.03^{\circ}\text{C/kPa}\).

From 10 kPa down to the triple‑point pressure (≈ 0.61 kPa) the expected change would therefore be only

\[
\Delta T \approx +0.03^{\circ}\text{C/kPa}\times(10-0.61)\,\text{kPa}
          \approx +0.30^{\circ}\text{C}.
\]

So even at 10 kPa the freezing point stays within ±0.3 °C of its ambient‑air value.

---

#### Bottom line

For practical purposes—and especially for engineering calculations involving liquids at moderate vacuum levels—you can treat the freezing point of water at 10 kPa as effectively **0 °C**. Only when approaching the triple point (below ~600 Pa) do significant deviations occur.
